title: Qatar Says Iran Is 'Fully Legally Responsible' for Attacking Its Tanker — AIS Data Shows the Tanker Was Loading Crude at a Sanctioned Iranian Terminal
narrative:
On July 7-8 2026, the United States launched over 80 strikes against Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz region, revoked Iran's oil sales license, and President Trump declared the June 17th ceasefire 'over' — calling Iranian leaders 'scum' and 'liars.' The stated trigger: Iran's IRGC had attacked three commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz on July 6-7, including the Qatari LNG tanker Al Rekayyat, which was described as an innocent commercial ship attacked without provocation. Qatar's foreign ministry formally blamed Iran, holding Tehran 'fully legally responsible' for what it called an 'unacceptable attack on international navigation and global energy security.' CENTCOM stated the attacks were 'a clear and dangerous violation of the ceasefire.'

The public narrative that Iran attacked an innocent LNG tanker in international waters collapses under AIS tracking data. Windward Ltd's maritime OSINT analysis — using AIS transponder records, draft changes, and satellite imagery cross-references — establishes the following physical timeline for Al Rekayyat (IMO 9397339):

The vessel went dark (switched off its AIS transponder) on June 18, 2026 — 19 days before the reported attack. It remained dark throughout. On July 6 at 23:14 UTC, while presenting as an LNG tanker 'in transit,' Al Rekayyat recorded a draft change from 9.6 meters to 12.4 meters — a physical indicator of cargo loading, inconsistent with an in-transit vessel. Windward's analysis assessed the vessel had been loading at Kharg Island, Iran's primary crude oil export terminal (which handles approximately 90% of Iran's oil exports), under the US-issued sanctions waiver that was revoked on July 7. The US Treasury issued the sanctions waiver on June 22, explicitly authorizing Iranian oil sales through August 21. The revocation on July 7 — within 24-48 hours of the AIS-tracked Kharg Island loading event — suggests US intelligence had detected the cargo operation via AIS/shore-based tracking and moved to cut off the revenue before Iran could complete the sale.

Windward separately identified a new Iranian sanctions evasion technique: 'asymmetric anchor-swing spoofing,' in which sanctioned dark-fleet vessels broadcast fabricated AIS tracks showing them anchored near the Iraq-Kuwait-Iran tri-border area while actually loading at Kharg Island. EO/SAR satellite imagery is required to expose this technique; AIS alone cannot detect it. Al Rekayyat was transiting via the NCAGS southern corridor — the same route Iran had designated as its approved safe passage lane — not the Omani route promoted by the US, UK, and France. GCap/Reuters confirmed the vessel's captain broadcast a mayday: 'We are being hit by drone on engine room.' The crew evacuated safely. No cargo loss reported.
analysis:
The US narrative frames the tanker attacks as unprovoked Iranian aggression against civilian shipping. The physical AIS record frames Al Rekayyat as a Qatari state vessel engaged in a dark-ship crude oil swap operation at Kharg Island — under a US-issued sanctions waiver that was revoked immediately upon detection of the loading. The sequence looks less like 'ceasefire violation' and more like a sanctions enforcement action that used the tanker-attack framing as political cover for pulling the license.

Qatar's foreign ministry called Iran 'fully legally responsible.' That statement is factually hollow given its own state-owned vessel was engaged in a dark-ship crude-oil-for-LNG swap at an Iranian terminal under a sanctions waiver that had not yet been revoked. Qatar knew, or should have known, that the Al Rekayyat's 19-day AIS blackout and draft change at Kharg Island would be detectable by US intelligence. When it was detected, the license was pulled within 24-48 hours. The attack on Al Rekayyat occurred — but the physical record suggests it occurred on a vessel that was mid-sanctions-evasion operation, not an innocent commercial tanker.

The load-bearing contradiction: the US framed this as an attack on innocent civilian LNG passage; the AIS data shows it was a crude-oil-for-LNG sanctions-swap operation at Kharg Island. The attack provided the political justification for revoking the waiver. The physical trail — 19-day AIS blackout, draft change at Kharg Island, near-simultaneous license revocation — is the evidence that the 'unprovoked attack' frame is incomplete.
verdict: The US had intelligence on Iran's sanctions evasion via AIS tracking and acted to cut off oil revenue. The attack narrative provided the political cover for the revocation. The physical trail of Al Rekayyat's 19-day AIS blackout and Kharg Island draft change is the evidence. Qatar's 'fully legally responsible' statement is hollow given its own vessel was engaged in the activity the US was trying to prohibit.
